To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

plague-endemic villages are associated with landscape variables (e.g., elevation, distance to the nearest river) and residential variables (e.g. presence of pigs and processed commercial foods) in the West Nile Region of Uganda.

plague is more prevalent in villages that are closer to the border with South Sudan (a country that has recently experienced plague outbreaks) and villages that are closer together, and that plague is more likely to be associated with huts that are close to other huts, huts that are closer to neighboring homesteads, huts that have pigs nearby, and huts with processed commercial food stored inside.

landscape-level and household-level variables associated with plague endemicity in West Nile region of northern Uganda include: 1) the distance of the hut from neighboring homesteads, 2) the presence of pigs near a hut, 3) the presence of annual crops (corn) near the hut, 4) water storage within the hut, and 5) the presence of processed commercial foods stored within the hut.
